L1305: … and a few surprises
L1306: Whereas the “seasonal” changes in the exosphere observed by MESSENGER were expected, there were a number of
L1307: discoveries during the flybys that were complete surprises.
L1308: During each flyby, a spacecraft roll was executed as MESSENGER entered Mercury’s shadow. This roll rotated the
L1309: look direction of the UVVS field of view about the Sun-Mercury line, carrying it from dawn through north to dusk in
L1310: the first two flybys and from south through dawn to just past north in the third flyby. In all three flybys, an equatorial
L1311: enhancement in the calcium distribution was seen in the dawn direction. This enhancement remains a mystery, not
L1312: just in terms of how it originates but also in its persistence across all three flybys. Despite differences in the space
L1313: environment among flybys that should have affected the source processes for calcium as they are currently understood,
L1314: this feature of the calcium distribution remained relatively unchanged in both location and intensity.
L1315: Other surprises came from the third flyby, which presented a special opportunity to observe the exosphere over the
L1316: polar regions. Altitude profiles of sodium, calcium, and magnesium were obtained over both the north and south poles.
L1317: Although it had been inferred from ground-based observations that sodium is released from the surface by both lowand high-energy processes, the clear two-component nature of the observed altitude profiles for sodium were the first
L1318: direct evidence that this is indeed the case. But more surprising were the profiles for magnesium. A distinctly different
L1319: profile was observed in the north compared to the south, and the structure in the northern profile cannot be fit with
L1320: the normal models applied to Mercury’s exosphere. This difference is even more startling when one considers the fact
L1321: that the calcium profiles show no such north-south difference. Both calcium and magnesium are refractory elements
L1322: and as such are expected to derive from similar processes in approximately the same manner. This is clearly not the case
L1323: over the north pole, and given the lack of an equatorial dawn enhancement in magnesium, the assumption that calcium
L1324: and magnesium will behave similarly is one that must be abandoned in favor of new ideas about the effect of several
L1325: contributory processes.
L1326: Perhaps the biggest surprise during the flybys, though, was the distribution of emission from ionized calcium. The
L1327: observation itself was the first observation of emission from an ionized species in Mercury’s exosphere. The ionized
L1328: calcium was observed to be concentrated close to equatorial plane in a narrow region 1–2 planetary radii tailward of
L1329: the planet. This distribution is inconsistent with local conversion of neutral calcium to ionized calcium, because there
L1330: is simply too much ionized calcium. Instead, the ionized calcium must be concentrated in that region by interaction
L1331: of the calcium ions with Mercury’s magnetosphere. The most likely explanation is that ions created on the dayside of
L1332: the planet, where there should be an abundance of photoions (ions created by sunlight hitting the neutral calcium
L1333: atoms), have been transported around Mercury to the tail region and concentrated by magnetospheric forces. The
L1334: magnetosphere was particularly active during the third flyby, so it remains to be seen whether this concentration was
L1335: specific to the conditions of the third flyby or will be observed during the orbital phase to be a regular phenomenon.
L1336: But one thing is clear: there is a greater degree of interaction between the exosphere and the magnetosphere than
L1337: previously suspected.

L1339: Mercury: An old world seen in new light
L1340: The three flybys of Mercury by MESSENGER in 2008 and 2009 produced more than 3,700 images (1,213 during flyby
L1341: 1, 1,287 during flyby 2, and 1,214 during flyby 3), more than 8,000 MLA range measurements (3,617 during flyby 1 and
L1342: 4,388 during flyby 2) for a profile length of 6,000 km on the surface, 20,000 UVVS spectra of the exosphere, 1,100 VIRS
L1343: spectra of the surface, and a host of other Magnetometer, GRNS, EPPS, XRS, and radio science data. With MESSENGER
L1344: already rewriting the textbooks on the innermost planet of the Solar System, a great deal more is to come with the
L1345: orbital phase of the mission.
L1346: The sixth and last planetary flyby of MESSENGER (including one of Earth, two of Venus, and three of Mercury) was
L1347: crucial for lining up the trajectory of MESSENGER for orbit insertion. Each Mercury flyby has extracted about 2 km/s
L1348: of speed from MESSENGER as it rapidly circles the Sun to reach near-synchronicity with Mercury’s own trajectory. Only
L1349: by matching speeds sufficiently closely by means of these flybys is MESSENGER’s own propulsion system capable of
L1350: completing the final braking maneuver into orbit in March 2011.

L1400: The Spacecraft
L1401: After Mariner 10’s visits to Mercury, the space science and engineering communities yearned for a longer and
L1402: more detailed look at the innermost planet — but that closer look, ideally from orbit, presented formidable technical
L1403: obstacles. A Mercury orbiter would have to be tough, with enough protection to withstand searing sunlight and roasting
L1404: heat bouncing back from the planet below. The spacecraft would need to be lightweight, since most of its mass would
L1405: be fuel to fire its rockets to slow the spacecraft down enough to be captured by Mercury’s gravity. And the probe would
L1406: have to be sufficiently compact to be launched on a conventional and cost-effective rocket.
L1407: Designed and built by the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) — with contributions from
L1408: research institutions and companies around the world — the MESSENGER spacecraft tackles each of these challenges.
L1409: A ceramic-fabric sunshade, heat radiators, and a mission design that limits time over the planet’s hottest regions protect
L1410: MESSENGER without expensive and impractical cooling systems. The spacecraft’s graphite composite structure — strong,
L1411: lightweight, and heat tolerant — is integrated with a low-mass propulsion system that efficiently stores and distributes
L1412: the approximately 600 kg of propellant that accounts for 54% of the total launch weight.
L1413: To fit behind the 2.5-m by 2-m sunshade, the wiring, electronics, systems, and instruments are packed into a small
L1414: frame that could fit inside a large sport utility vehicle. And the entire spacecraft is light enough to launch on a Delta II
L1415: 7925H-9.5 (“heavy”) rocket, the largest launch vehicle allowed under NASA’s Discovery Program of lower-cost space
L1416: science missions. MESSENGER spacecraft during integration and testing. The sunshade is visible on the left with the
L1417: spacecraft undergoing testing in thermal-vacuum conditions at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. On
L1418: the right, the solar panels and Magnetometer boom are in their position for flight during work at APL.

L1420: Science payload
L1421: MESSENGER carries seven scientific instruments and a radio science experiment to accomplish an ambitious objective:
L1422: return the first data from Mercury orbit. The miniaturized payload — designed to work in the extreme environment
L1423: near the Sun — will image the entire surface of Mercury, as well as gather data on the composition and structure of
L1424: Mercury’s crust, its geologic history, the nature of its active magnetosphere and thin atmosphere, and the makeup of its
L1425: core and the materials near its poles.
L1426: The instruments include the Mercury Dual Imaging System (MDIS), the Gamma-Ray and Neutron Spectrometer
L1427: (GRNS), the X-Ray Spectrometer (XRS), the Magnetometer (MAG), the Mercury Laser Altimeter (MLA), the Mercury
L1428: Atmospheric and Surface Composition Spectrometer (MASCS), and the Energetic Particle and Plasma Spectrometer
L1429: (EPPS). The instruments communicate to the spacecraft through fully redundant Data Processing Units (DPUs).
L1430: The process of selecting the scientific instrumentation for a mission is typically a balance between answering as
L1431: many science questions as possible and fitting within the available mission resources for mass, power, mechanical
L1432: accommodation, schedule, and cost. In the case of MESSENGER, the mass and mechanical accommodation issues were
L1433: very significant constraints. Payload mass was limited to 50 kg because of the propellant mass needed for orbit insertion.
L1434: The instrument mechanical accommodation was difficult because of the unique thermal constraints faced during the
L1435: mission; instruments had to be mounted where Mercury would be in view but the Sun would not, and they had to be
L1436: maintained within an acceptable temperature range in a very harsh environment. Instrument details follow. In each case

L1595: Spacecraft systems and components
L1596: Thermal Design
L1597: While orbiting Mercury, MESSENGER will “feel” significantly hotter than spacecraft that orbit Earth. This is because
L1598: Mercury’s elongated orbit swings the planet to within 46 million km of the Sun, or about two-thirds closer to the Sun
L1599: than Earth. As a result, the Sun shines up to 11 times brighter at Mercury than we see from our own planet.
L1600: MESSENGER’s first line of thermal defense is a heat-resistant and highly reflective sunshade, fixed on a titanium frame
L1601: to the front of the spacecraft. Measuring about 2.5 m tall and 2 m across as viewed head-on, the thin shade has front
L1602: and back layers of Nextel ceramic cloth — the same material that protects sections of the Space Shuttle — surrounding
L1603: several inner layers of Kapton plastic insulation. While temperatures on the front of the shade could reach 370° C when
L1604: Mercury is closest to the Sun, behind it the spacecraft will operate at room temperature, around 20° C.
L1605: As the second line of defense against this challenging environment, the science orbit is designed to limit
L1606: MESSENGER’s exposure to the heat re-radiating from the surface of Mercury. (MESSENGER will only spend about 25
L1607: minutes of each 12-hour orbit crossing Mercury’s broiling surface at low altitude.) Multilayered insulation covers most of
L1608: MESSENGER spacecraft in flight configuration, rear view
L1609: 
L1610: the surfaces of the spacecraft to protect against incident thermal radiation and insulate against internal heat loss, and
L1611: radiators connected to diode (“one-way”) heat pipes are installed on the sides of the spacecraft to carry heat away from
L1612: the spacecraft body. The combination of the sunshade, unique orbital design, thermal blanketing, and heat-radiation
L1613: system allows the spacecraft to operate without special high-temperature electronics.
L1614: Power
L1615: Two single-sided solar panels are the spacecraft’s main source of electric power. To run MESSENGER’s systems and
L1616: charge its 23-ampere-hour nickel-hydrogen battery, the panels, each about 1.5 m by 1.75 m in extent, will support
L1617: between 440 and 475 W of spacecraft load power during the cruise phase and 650 W during the orbit at Mercury. The
L1618: panels themselves produce more than 2 kW of power near Mercury, but to prevent stress on MESSENGER’s electronics
L1619: and keep operating temperatures within acceptable limits, onboard power processors convert only what the spacecraft
L1620: was designed to consume in orbit.
L1621: The custom-developed panels are two-thirds mirrors (called optical solar reflectors) and one-third triple-junction solar
L1622: cells, which convert 28% of the sunlight hitting them into electricity. Each panel has two rows of mirrors for every row
L1623: of cells; the small mirrors reflect the Sun’s energy and keep the panel cooler. The panels also rotate, so the operations
L1624: team tilts the panels away from the Sun, positioning them to get the required power while maintaining a normal surface
L1625: operating temperature of about 150° C.
L1626: Propulsion
L1627: MESSENGER’s dual-mode propulsion system includes a 660-N bipropellant thruster for large maneuvers and 16
L1628: hydrazine-propellant thrusters for smaller trajectory adjustments and attitude control. The Large Velocity Adjust (LVA)
L1629: thruster requires a combination of hydrazine fuel and nitrogen tetroxide oxidizer. Fuel and oxidizer are stored in customdesigned, lightweight titanium tanks integrated into the spacecraft’s composite frame. Helium pressurizes the system
L1630: and pushes the fuel and oxidizer through to the engines.
L1631: At launch the spacecraft carried just under 600 kg of propellant, and it will use nearly 30% of it during the maneuver
L1632: that inserts the spacecraft into orbit around Mercury. The hydrazine thrusters play several important roles: four 22-N
L1633: thrusters are used for small course corrections and help steady MESSENGER during large engine burns. The dozen 4.4-N
L1634: thrusters are also used for small course corrections and also help steady the spacecraft during all propulsive maneuvers.
L1635: These smallest thrusters can also serve as a backup for the reaction wheels that maintain the spacecraft’s orientation
L1636: during normal cruise and orbital operations.
L1637: Communications
L1638: MESSENGER’s X-band coherent communications system includes two high-gain, electronically steered, phased-array
L1639: antennas — the first ever used on a deep-space mission; two medium-gain fanbeam antennas; and four low-gain
L1640: antennas. The circularly polarized phased arrays — developed by APL and located with the fanbeam antennas on the
L1641: front and back of the spacecraft — are the main link for sending science data back to Earth. For better reliability in the
L1642: high-temperature environment the antennas are fixed; they “point” electronically across a 45° field of regard without
L1643: moving parts.
L1644: High-gain antennas send radio signals through a narrower, more concentrated beam than medium- or low-gain
L1645: antennas and are used to send large amounts of data over the same distance as a lower-gain antenna. The fanbeam
L1646: antennas, also located on MESSENGER’s front and back sides, are used for lower-rate data transmissions to the Earth
L1647: as well as nominal command transmissions from the Earth, such as operating commands, status data, or emergency
L1648: communications. The four low-gain antennas provide hemispheric fields of view from the top, bottom, front, and
L1649: back of the spacecraft, providing primarily an emergency bi-directional communications link with the Earth in the
L1650: event attitude knowledge is lost. MESSENGER’s downlink rate ranges from 9.9 bits per second to 104 kilobits per
L1651: second; operators can send commands at 7.8 to 500 bits per second. Transmission rates vary according to onboard
L1652: communications system configuration, spacecraft distance from the Earth, and ground-station antenna size.

L1654: Command and Data Handling
L1655: MESSENGER’s “brain” is its Integrated Electronics Module (IEM), a space- and weight-saving device that combines
L1656: the spacecraft’s core avionics into a single box. The spacecraft carries a pair of identical IEMs for backup purposes; both
L1657: house a 25-MHz main processor and 10-MHz fault-protection processor. All four are radiation-hardened RAD6000
L1658: processors, based on predecessors of the PowerPC chip found in some models of home computers. The computers,
L1659: slow by current home-computer standards, are state of the art for the radiation tolerance required on the MESSENGER
L1660: mission.
L1661: Programmed to monitor the condition of MESSENGER’s key systems, both fault-protection processors are turned
L1662: on at all times and protect the spacecraft by turning off components and/or switching to backup components when
L1663: necessary. The main processor runs the command and data handling software for data transfer and file storage, as well
L1664: as the guidance and control software used to navigate and point the spacecraft. Each IEM also includes a solid-state
L1665: data recorder, power converters, and the interfaces between the processors and MESSENGER’s instruments and systems.
L1666: Intricate flight software executes MESSENGER’s Command and Data Handling system. MESSENGER receives operating
L1667: commands from Earth and can perform them in real time or store them for later execution. Most of the frequent,
L1668: critical operations (such as propulsive maneuvers) are programmed into the flight computer’s memory and timed to run
L1669: automatically.
L1670: For data, MESSENGER carries two solid-state recorders (one backup) able to store up to 1 gigabyte each. The main
L1671: processor collects, compresses, and stores images and other data from the subsystems and instruments onto the
L1672: recorder; the software sorts the data into files in a manner similar to how files are stored on a PC. The main processor
L1673: selects the files with highest priority to transmit to Earth, or mission operators can download data files in any order the
L1674: team chooses.
L1675: In orbit around Mercury, data downlink rates will vary predominantly with spacecraft-to-Earth distance. Thus when
L1676: orbiting Mercury, MESSENGER will store most of its data when it’s farther from Earth, typically sending only information
L1677: on its condition and the highest-priority images and measurements during contacts through NASA’s Deep Space
L1678: Network. The spacecraft will send most of the recorded data when Mercury’s path around the Sun brings it closer to
L1679: Earth.
L1680: Guidance and Control
L1681: MESSENGER is well protected against the heat, but it must always know its orientation relative to Mercury, Earth,
L1682: and the Sun and be “smart” enough to keep its sunshade pointed at the Sun. Attitude determination — knowing in
L1683: which direction MESSENGER is facing — is performed using star-tracking cameras, digital Sun sensors, and an inertial
L1684: measurement unit (IMU), which contains gyroscopes and accelerometers). Attitude control for the three-axis stabilized
L1685: craft is accomplished using four internal reaction wheels and, when necessary, MESSENGER’s small thrusters.
L1686: The IMU accurately determines the spacecraft’s rotation rate, and MESSENGER tracks its own orientation by checking
L1687: the location of stars and the Sun. Star-tracking cameras on MESSENGER’s top deck store a complete map of the
L1688: heavens; once a second, one of the cameras takes a wide-angle picture of space, compares the locations of stars to its
L1689: onboard map, and then calculates the spacecraft’s orientation. The guidance and control software also automatically
L1690: rotates the solar panels to the commanded Sun-relative orientation, as the spacecraft body rotates, ensuring that the
L1691: panels produce sufficient power while maintaining safe temperatures.
L1692: The suite of Sun sensors backs up the star trackers, continuously measuring MESSENGER’s angle to the Sun. If the
L1693: flight software detects that the Sun is “moving” out of a designated safe zone, it can initiate an automatic turn to
L1694: ensure that the shade faces the Sun. Ground controllers can then analyze the situation while the spacecraft turns its
L1695: antennas to Earth and awaits instructions — an operating condition known as “safe” mode.

L1784: Mission Summary
L1785: Cruise trajectory
L1786: The MESSENGER mission takes advantage of an ingenious
L1787: trajectory design, lightweight materials, and miniaturization
L1788: of electronics, all developed in the three decades since
L1789: Mariner 10 flew past Mercury in 1974 and 1975. The
L1790: compact orbiter, fortified against the searing conditions
L1791: near the Sun, will investigate key questions about Mercury’s
L1792: characteristics and environment with a set of seven scientific
L1793: instruments.
L1794: On a 7.9-billion-km journey that included more than
L1795: 15 loops	around	the	Sun,	the	spacecraft’ s	trajectory	included
L1796: one pass by Earth, two by Venus, and three by Mercury,
L1797: before a propulsive burn will ease it into orbit around its
L1798: target planet. The Earth flyby in August 2005, along with
L1799: the Venus flybys in October 2006 and June 2007 and the
L1800: three Mercury flybys in January 2008, October 2008, and
L1801: September 2009 used the pull of each planet’s gravity to
L1802: guide MESSENGER toward Mercury’s orbit.
L1803: The combined effect of the six gravity assists from three
L1804: planets and five deterministic deep-space maneuvers (DSMs)
L1805: — using the bipropellant Large Velocity Adjust (LVA) engine
L1806: of the spacecraft and the influence of the Sun — accelerated
L1807: the spacecraft from an average speed around the Sun of
L1808: 30 km/s	(the	Earth’ s	average	speed	around	the	Sun)	to
L1809: 48 km/s	(Mercury’ s	average	speed	around	the	Sun).
L1810: The cruise phase of the mission concludes in March 2011,
L1811: when the spacecraft will execute the Mercury orbit insertion
L1812: (MOI) maneuver, slowing the spacecraft and allowing it to
L1813: be captured into orbit around Mercury.
L1814: Getting a Boost
L1815: For a gravity assist, a spacecraft flies close to
L1816: a planet and trades with the planet’s orbital
L1817: momentum around the Sun. Depending on the
L1818: relative difference in mass between the planet
L1819: and the spacecraft, as well as the distance
L1820: between the two, this exchange of momentum
L1821: can impart a substantial change in spacecraft
L1822: speed. Since the spacecraft’s mass is negligible
L1823: compared with that of the planet, this process
L1824: has a negligible effect on the planet’s orbit
L1825: around the Sun. But the spacecraft receives a
L1826: great boost on the way to its next destination.
L1827: Gravity-assist maneuvers can be used to speed
L1828: a spacecraft up or slow a spacecraft down.
L1829: Closest approach distance, direction, and the
L1830: velocity of a spacecraft relative to the planet’s
L1831: velocity all affect the acceleration magnitude and
L1832: direction change of the spacecraft’s trajectory.
L1833: The greatest change in a spacecraft’s speed and
L1834: direction occurs when a slow-moving spacecraft
L1835: approaches just above the surface or cloud
L1836: tops of a massive planet. The least change in a
L1837: spacecraft’s speed and direction occurs when
L1838: a fast-moving spacecraft approaches a small
L1839: planet from a great distance.

L1844: Multiple Flybys
L1845: Mariner 10 flew past Venus to reach Mercury, but the idea of multiple Venus/Mercury flybys to help
L1846: a spacecraft “catch” Mercury and begin orbiting the planet came years later, when Chen-wan Yen of
L1847: NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory developed the concept in the mid-1980s. MESSENGER adopted this
L1848: mission design approach; without these flybys, MESSENGER would move so fast past Mercury that no
L1849: existing propulsion system could slow it down sufficiently for it to be captured into orbit.
L1850: 
L1851: Launch
L1852: MESSENGER launched from Pad B of Space Launch Complex 17 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Fla., on a threestage Boeing Delta II expendable launch vehicle on August 3, 2004. The Delta II 7925H-9.5 (heavy lift) model was the
L1853: largest allowed for NASA Discovery missions. It features a liquid-fueled first stage with nine strap-on solid boosters, a
L1854: second-stage liquid-fueled engine, and a third-stage solid-fuel rocket. With MESSENGER secured in a 9.5-m fairing on
L1855: top, the launch vehicle was about 40 m tall.
L1856: The launch vehicle imparted an excess launch energy per mass (usually denoted by C3 and equal to the excess over
L1857: what is required for Earth escape) of approximately 16.4 km2/s2 to the spacecraft, setting up the spacecraft for a return
L1858: pass by the Earth approximately one year from launch.
L1859: Earth flyby highlights
L1860: MESSENGER swung by its home planet on August 2, 2005, for a gravity assist that propelled it deeper into the inner
L1861: Solar System. MESSENGER’s systems performed flawlessly as the spacecraft swooped around Earth, coming to a closest
L1862: approach point of about 2,348 km over central Mongolia at 3:13 p.m. EDT. The spacecraft used the tug of Earth’s
L1863: gravity to change its trajectory significantly, bringing its average orbital distance nearly 29 million km closer to the Sun
L1864: and sending it toward Venus for gravity assists in 2006 and 2007.
L1865: Team members in the MESSENGER Mission Operations Center at APL watch the spacecraft launch from Cape
L1866: Canaveral. The team began operating the spacecraft less than an hour later, after MESSENGER separated
L1867: from the launch vehicle.

L1878: MESSENGER’s main camera snapped several approach shots of Earth and the Moon, including a series of color images
L1879: that science team members strung into a “movie” documenting MESSENGER’s departure. On approach, the Mercury
L1880: Atmospheric and Surface Composition Spectrometer (MASCS) also made several scans of the Moon in conjunction with
L1881: the camera observations, and during the flyby the particle and magnetic field instruments spent several hours making
L1882: measurements in Earth’s magnetosphere.
L1883: The close flyby of Earth and the Moon allowed MESSENGER to give its two Mercury Dual Imaging System (MDIS)
L1884: cameras a thorough workout. The images helped the team understand fully how the cameras operate in flight in
L1885: comparison with test results obtained in the laboratory before launch. Images were taken in full color and at different
L1886: resolutions, and the cameras passed their tests.
L1887: Not only were these pictures useful for carefully calibrating the imagers for the spacecraft’s Mercury encounters, they
L1888: also offered a unique view of Earth. Through clear skies over much of South America, features such as the Amazon, the
L1889: Andes, and Lake Titicaca are visible, as are huge swaths of rain forest.
L1890: The pictures from MESSENGER’s flyby of Earth include “natural” color and infrared views of North and South
L1891: America; a peek at the Galápagos Islands through a break in the clouds; and the movie of the rotating Earth, taken as
L1892: MESSENGER sped away from its home planet.
L1893: Using various combinations of filters in the optical path, MESSENGER’s camera can obtain a mix of
L1894: red, green, and blue (RGB) light in various proportions to create a full spectrum of colors. On the left
L1895: is a “normal” color image of the Earth. On the right, infrared images are visualized by substituting
L1896: one of the RGB components. Continental areas are mostly red due to the high reflectance of
L1897: vegetation in the near-infrared. Short-wavelength light (blue) is easily scattered in Earth’s atmosphere,
L1898: producing our blue skies, but also obscuring the surface from MESSENGER’s viewpoint. Infrared light
L1899: is not easily scattered, so images of the Earth remain sharp.

L1902: Venus gravity assists
L1903: MESSENGER has flown by Venus twice using the tug of the planet’s gravity to change its trajectory, to shrink the
L1904: spacecraft’s orbit around the Sun, and to bring it closer to Mercury.
L1905: During the first Venus flyby on October 24, 2006, the spacecraft came within 2,987 km of the surface of Venus.
L1906: Shortly before the encounter, MESSENGER entered superior solar conjunction, where it was on the opposite side of the
L1907: Sun from Earth and during which reliable communication between MESSENGER and mission operators was not possible.
L1908: In addition, during the flyby the spacecraft experienced the mission’s first and longest eclipse of the Sun by a planet.
L1909: During the eclipse, which lasted approximately 56 minutes, the spacecraft’s solar arrays were in the shadow of Venus
L1910: and MESSENGER operated on battery power.
L1911: MESSENGER swung by Venus for the second time on June 5, 2007, speeding over the planet’s cloud tops at a
L1912: relative velocity of more than 48,000 km/hour and passing within 338 km of its surface near the boundary between the
L1913: lowland plains of Rusalka Planitia and the rifted uplands of Aphrodite Terra. The maneuver sharpened the spacecraft’s
L1914: aim toward the first encounter with Mercury and presented a special opportunity to calibrate several of its science
L1915: instruments and learn something new about Earth’s nearest neighbor.

L1929: All of the MESSENGER instruments operated during the flyby. The camera system imaged the nightside in nearinfrared bands and obtained color and higher-resolution monochrome mosaics of both the approaching and departing
L1930: hemispheres. The ultraviolet and visible spectrometer on the MASCS instrument obtained profiles of atmospheric species
L1931: on the day and night sides as well as observations of the exospheric tail on departure.
L1932: The MASCS visible and infrared spectrometer observed the Venus dayside near closest approach to gather
L1933: compositional information on the upper atmosphere and clouds, and the Mercury Laser Altimeter (MLA) carried out
L1934: passive radiometry and attempted to range to the Venus upper atmosphere and clouds for several minutes near closest
L1935: approach. The Gamma-Ray and Neutron Spectrometer (GRNS) instrument observed gamma-rays and neutrons from
L1936: Venus’ atmosphere, providing information for planning the upcoming Mercury flybys and for calibration from a source of
L1937: known composition.
L1938: The European Space Agency’s Venus Express mission was operating at the time of the flyby, permitting the
L1939: simultaneous observation of the planet from two independent spacecraft, a situation of particular value for
L1940: characterization of the particle-and-field environment at Venus. MESSENGER’s Energetic Particle and Plasma
L1941: Spectrometer (EPPS) observed charged particle acceleration at the Venus bow shock and elsewhere, and the
L1942: Magnetometer (MAG) measured the upstream interplanetary magnetic field (IMF), bow shock signatures, and pick-up
L1943: ion waves as a reference for energetic particle and plasma observations by both spacecraft. The encounter also enabled
L1944: two-point measurements of IMF penetration into the Venus ionosphere, primary plasma boundaries, and the near-tail
L1945: region.

L1954: Flying by Mercury
L1955: On January 14, 2008, at 19:04:39 UTC (2:04:39 p.m. EST) the MESSENGER spacecraft executed its first Mercury flyby,
L1956: passing over the uncharted surface of the planet at an altitude of 201.4 km, an even more accurate aim than for the
L1957: second Venus flyby. The primary purpose of this activity was to shrink the orbital period of the spacecraft around the
L1958: Sun by 11 days, bringing MESSENGER’s orbit closer to Mercury’s orbit. On October 6, 2008, at 08:40:22 UTC (4:40:22
L1959: EDT) the MESSENGER spacecraft executed its second Mercury flyby, passing above the surface at an altitude of 199.2
L1960: km, within a phenomenal 760 meters of the planned flyby altitude! Although the flyby enabled direct observation of
L1961: additional previously unobserved planetary surface features, the primary purpose of the flyby was to shrink the orbital
L1962: period of the spacecraft around the Sun by an additional 16 days and increase the ecliptic inclination of the spacecraft
L1963: by 0.1 degrees, further matching the orbit of Mercury around the Sun. The third and final Mercury flyby on September
L1964: 29, 2009, at 21:54:56 UTC (5:54:56 p.m. EST) further decreased the spacecraft’s orbital period around the Sun by
L1965: almost 13 days to 104.8 days, and increased the inclination of the spacecraft’s orbit by a tiny amount (0.001º) such that
L1966: it now closely matches Mercury’s 7.0 degree orbit inclination. The spacecraft’s lowest altitude above the planet was
L1967: 227.5 kilometers. These adjustments to the spacecraft’s orbit will enable it to enter orbit about Mercury on March 18,
L1968: 2011 UTC.
L1969: In conjunction with these flyby activities, pre-determined course-correction maneuvers — deep-space maneuvers
L1970: (DSMs) using the main Large Velocity Adjust (LVA) engine — were scheduled approximately two months after each flyby
L1971: to adjust further the spacecraft trajectory in preparation for the eventual capture into orbit around Mercury.
L1972: Mercury Flybys
L1973: North ecliptic pole view of the trajectory between the first Mercury flyby and Mercury orbit insertion. Dashed
L1974: lines depict the orbits of Earth, Venus, and Mercury. Timeline fading helps emphasize primary events.
L1975: 
L1976: As a result of the three flybys of Mercury, MESSENGER has viewed nearly 91% of the entire planet in color, imaged
L1977: most of the areas not seen by Mariner 10, and taken measurements of the composition of the surface, atmosphere, and
L1978: magnetosphere. In contrast to the orbital phase of the mission, the closest approach points during the flybys were on
L1979: the night side and near the planet’s equator. These approaches provide special vantages to gather high-resolution images
L1980: of the low- to mid-latitude regions of the planet as well as low-latitude measurements of the magnetic and gravitational
L1981: fields.
L1982: Mercury Flybys
L1983: View of the three Mercury flyby trajectories from above the planet’s northern pole. The yellow line marks the
L1984: position of the day/night or dawn/dusk terminator. Closest approach time listed is in local spacecraft time, not
L1985: accounting for the one-way light time for the signals to reach the Earth.

L1987: MESSENGER’s deep-space maneuvers
L1988: In conjunction with the six planetary flybys, MESSENGER’s complex 6.6-year cruise trajectory has included more than
L1989: 40 anticipated trajectory-correction maneuvers (TCMs). These TCMs included five deterministic deep-space maneuvers
L1990: (DSMs), which used the spacecraft’s bipropellant Large Velocity Adjust (LVA) engine. In addition to imparting a combined
L1991: spacecraft change in velocity of more than 1 km/s, the DSMs were the primary method used to target the spacecraft
L1992: before each planetary flyby (except the second Venus flyby). Smaller velocity-adjustment maneuvers that used the
L1993: propulsion system’s monopropellant thrusters fine-tuned the trajectory between the main DSMs and the gravity-assist
L1994: flybys of the planets.
L1995: On December 12, 2005, MESSENGER successfully fired its bipropellant LVA engine for the first time, completing the
L1996: first of the five critical deep-space maneuvers (DSM-1). The maneuver, just over 8 minutes long, changed MESSENGER’s
L1997: speed by approximately 316 m/s, placing the spacecraft on target for the first Venus flyby on October 24, 2006.
L1998: This maneuver was the first to rely solely on the LVA, the largest and most efficient engine of the propulsion system.
L1999: Maneuvers performed with the LVA use about 30% less total propellant mass — both fuel and oxidizer — than the
L2000: other thrusters, which use monopropellant fuel only. Approximately 100 kg of propellant (both fuel and oxidizer), about
L2001: 18% of the total onboard propellant, was used to complete DSM-1.
L2002: On October 17, 2007, MESSENGER completed its second critical DSM — 250 million km from Earth — successfully
L2003: firing the LVA again to change the spacecraft’s trajectory and target it for its historic flyby of Mercury on January 14,
L2004: 2008. The maneuver, just over 5 minutes long, consumed approximately 70 kg of propellant (both fuel and oxidizer),
L2005: changing the velocity of the spacecraft by approximately 226 m/s.
L2006: On March 19, 2008, MESSENGER completed its third critical DSM, successfully firing the LVA once again to change
L2007: the spacecraft’s trajectory and target it for the second flyby of Mercury on October 6, 2008. The shortest deterministic
L2008: maneuver for the mission on the LVA, just over 2.5 minutes long, consumed approximately 21 kg of propellant (both
L2009: fuel and oxidizer), changing the velocity of the spacecraft by approximately 72 m/s.
L2010: On December 4 and 8, 2008, MESSENGER completed its fourth critical DSM, successfully firing the LVA twice to
L2011: adjust the spacecraft’s trajectory and target it for the third flyby of Mercury on September 29, 2009. This maneuver
L2012: was purposely split into two parts to provide engineers a practice opportunity for the cruise-ending Mercury Orbit
L2013: Insertion maneuver. Combined, the two parts of this DSM consumed about 68 kg of propellant over a total firing time
L2014: of	6.5 minutes,	changing	the	spacecraft	velocity	by	222	m/s	and	then	by	25	m/s,	respectively,	for	each	part	of	the
L2015: maneuver.
L2016: MESSENGER completed its fifth and final critical DSM on November 24, 2009. This maneuver, which lasted
L2017: 4.6 minutes,	changed	the	spacecraft’ s	velocity	by	178	m/s	and	used	approximately	46	kg	of	propellant.

L2129: Program/Project Management
L2130: Sean C. Solomon of the Carnegie Institution of Washington (CIW) leads the MESSENGER mission as the Principal
L2131: Investigator. The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (APL), Laurel, Md., manages the MESSENGER
L2132: mission for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, Washington, D.C.
L2133: At NASA Headquarters, Edward J. Weiler is the Associate Administrator for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate.
L2134: James L. Green is the Director of that directorate’s Planetary Science Division. Anthony Carro is the MESSENGER Program
L2135: Executive, and Edwin J. Grayzeck is the MESSENGER Program Scientist. The NASA Discovery Program is managed out
L2136: of the Marshall Space Flight Center, where Dennon J. Clardy is the Discovery Program Manager, and James E. Lee is the
L2137: MESSENGER Mission Manager.
L2138: At APL, Peter D. Bedini is the MESSENGER Project Manager, Ralph L. McNutt, Jr., is Project Scientist, Eric J. Finnegan is
L2139: the Mission Systems Engineer, and Andrew B. Calloway is the Mission Operations Manager.
L2140: NASA Discovery Program
L2141: MESSENGER is the seventh mission in NASA’s Discovery Program of lower-cost, highly focused, planetary science
L2142: investigations. Created in 1992, Discovery challenges teams of scientists and engineers to find innovative and
L2143: imaginative ways to uncover the mysteries of the Solar System within limited, cost-capped budgets and schedules.
L2144: Other Discovery missions
L2145: NEAR (Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous) marked the Discovery Program’s first launch, in February 1996. The NEAR
L2146: Shoemaker spacecraft became the first to orbit an asteroid when it reached 433 Eros in February 2000. After collecting
L2147: 10 times the data initially expected during a year around Eros, in February 2001, NEAR Shoemaker became the first
L2148: spacecraft to land on an asteroid and collect data from its surface.
L2149: Mars Pathfinder launched December 1996 and landed on Mars in July 1997. The mission demonstrated several
L2150: tools and techniques for future Mars missions — such as entering, descending, and landing with airbags to deliver a
L2151: robotic rover — while captivating the world with color pictures from the red planet.
L2152: Lunar Prospector orbited Earth’s Moon for 18 months after launching in January 1998. The mission’s data enabled
L2153: scientists to create detailed maps of the gravity, magnetic properties, and chemical makeup of the Moon’s entire surface.
L2154: Stardust, launched in February 1999, collected samples of comet dust and provided the closest look yet at a comet
L2155: nucleus when it sailed through the coma of Wild 2 in January 2004. It returned the cometary dust to Earth in January
L2156: 2006.
L2157: Genesis, launched in August 2001, collected solar wind particles and returned them to Earth in September 2004.
L2158: The samples are improving our understanding of the isotopic composition of the Sun, information that will help to
L2159: identify what the young Solar System was like.
L2160: CONTOUR (Comet Nucleus Tour) was designed to fly past and study at least two very different comets as they visited
L2161: the inner Solar System. The spacecraft was lost six weeks after launch, during a critical rocket-firing maneuver in August
L2162: 2002 to boost it from Earth’s orbit onto a comet-chasing path around the Sun.
L2163: Deep Impact, launched in January 2005, was the first experiment to probe beneath the surface of a comet,
L2164: attempting to reveal never-before-seen materials that would provide clues to the internal composition and structure
L2165: of a comet. In July 2005, a variety of instruments, both onboard the spacecraft and at ground-based and space-based
L2166: observatories around the world, observed the impact with the comet and examined the resulting debris and interior
L2167: material.
L2168: 
L2169: Dawn, launched in September 2007 toward Vesta and Ceres, two of the largest main-belt asteroids in our Solar
L2170: System, will provide key data on asteroid properties by orbiting and observing these minor planets. Dawn is scheduled to
L2171: arrive at Vesta in July 2011.
L2172: Kepler, launched in March 2009, is monitoring 100,000 stars similar to our Sun for four years, using new technology
L2173: to search local regions of the galaxy for Earth-size (or smaller) planets for the first time.
L2174: The GRAIL (Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory) mission, scheduled to launch in September 2011, will fly twin
L2175: spacecraft in tandem orbits around the Moon for several months to measure its gravity field in unprecedented detail.
L2176: The mission also will answer longstanding questions about Earth’s Moon and provide scientists a better understanding of
L2177: how Earth and other rocky planets in the Solar System formed.
L2178: Discovery also includes Missions of Opportunity — not complete Discovery missions, but pieces of a larger NASA or
L2179: non-NASA mission or creative reuses of spacecraft that have completed their prime missions. Those selected to date for
L2180: flight include:
L2181: •	 The	ASPERA-3 (Analyzer of Space Plasma and Energetic Atoms) instrument is studying the interaction between the
L2182: solar wind and the Martian atmosphere from the European Space Agency’s Mars Express spacecraft, which began
L2183: orbiting Mars in December 2003.
L2184: •	 The	M3 (Moon Mineralogy Mapper), pronounced M-cubed, is one of eleven instruments that flew onboard
L2185: Chandrayaan-1, which launched in October 2008. Chandrayaan-1, India’s first deep space mission, was a project of
L2186: the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). The goals of the mission included expanding scientific knowledge of
L2187: the Moon, upgrading India’s technological capability, and providing challenging opportunities for planetary research
L2188: for the younger generation.
L2189: •	 The	EPOXI mission combines two science investigations — the Extrasolar Planet Observation and Characterization
L2190: (EPOCh) and the Deep Impact Extended Investigation (DIXI). Both investigations are using the Deep Impact spacecraft,
L2191: which finished its prime mission in 2005. EPOCh is using the Deep Impact spacecraft to observe several nearby bright
L2192: stars for transits by orbiting planets, and DIXI involved the successful flyby of comet Hartley 2 in October 2010.
L2193: •	 NExT (New Exploration of Tempel 1) reused NASA’s Stardust spacecraft to revisit comet Tempel 1, the cometary
L2194: target of Deep Impact, in February 2011. This investigation provided the first look at the changes to a comet nucleus
L2195: produced after its close approach to the Sun.
L2196: •	 STROFIO (Start from a ROtating FIeld mass spectrOmeter) is a mass spectrometer that is part of the SERENA (Search
L2197: Exospheric Refilling and Emitted Natural Abundances) instrument package selected to fly on the European Space
L2198: Agency’s BepiColombo Mercury Planetary Orbiter spacecraft, scheduled to launch in 2014. The SERENA instrument
L2199: has two neutral particle analyzers (STROFIO and ELENA) and two ion spectrometers (MICA and PICAM). STROFIO,
L2200: from the Greek word “strofi” (to rotate), will determine the composition of Mercury’s exosphere.
L2201: For more on the Discovery Program, visit http://discovery.nasa.gov.

제공된 원문만 읽고 질문에 필요한 사실을 최대 8행의 표로 추출하라. 아직 원고를 쓰지 마라. subject는 사실의 주체, relation은 관계/특성, comparison_target은 비교 대상, value는 수치 표현, unit은 단위, basis는 비율의 기준/분모/설계목표·실제결과 구분이다. 원문에 없는 값은 추정하지 말고 빈 문자열로 둔다. 숫자가 없는 사실도 기록할 수 있다. 주체·비교대상·수치·단위는 원문 영어 표현을 그대로 쓰고 relation/basis/reason은 한국어로 쓴다. 각 행은 하나의 사실과 하나의 연속된 수치 표현만 담아라. 떨어진 두 수치를 세미콜론 등으로 합치지 말고 별도 행으로 분리하라. 선택 줄에 주체 이름이 없다면 이름이 나오는 앞뒤 문맥까지 포함하라. relation과 basis에 다른 언어 설명을 섞지 마라. subject에는 문서 제목의 임무명을 반복하기보다 선택 줄에 실제 쓰인 명사구나 대명사를 그대로 적어도 된다. 문서명은 별도로 보존된다. 수치와 그 수치의 주체를 포함하는 시작/끝 줄을 선택하라. 다른 장비의 정보로 질문 대상의 성과를 대신하지 마라. 필요한 사실이 빠지면 insufficient=true로 누락된 항목을 reason에 명시하라. 반드시 지정된 JSON Schema 객체 하나만 반환하라.
맡은 절과 다른 연구원의 구역이 지정돼 있으면 부족 신고는 자기 절의 지시 범위로 판단하라. 다른 연구원이 맡은 자료가 자기 입력에 없다는 사실만으로 자기 절을 부족하다고 신고하지 마라.

L135: Venus, the ‘Morning Star’ , the second closest
L136: planet to the Sun after Mercury and our
L137: closest planetary neighbour, has fascinated
L138: mankind from the earliest times. Named
L139: after the Roman goddess of love and
L140: beauty, it is the third brightest object in the
L141: sky after the Sun and the Moon.
L142: Since the beginning of the space era, Venus
L143: has been an attractive subject for planetary
L144: science and it was one of the first natural
L145: targets to explore, due to its proximity to
L146: Earth – half as far as Mars at closest
L147: approach. Very similar to Earth in size and
L148: mass, Venus was expected to be very like to
L149: our own planet when the first Russian and
L150: American space probes approached it in
L151: the early 1960s and started returning the
L152: first data about its atmosphere.
L153: Observers soon realised that Venus is an
L154: entirely different, exotic and inhospitable
L155: world, hidden behind a curtain of dense
L156: clouds of noxious gases. It has an
L157: atmosphere composed mainly of carbon
L158: dioxide, with a crushing surface pressure
L159: and burning-hot temperatures. The
L160: question then arose: Why did a planet
L161: apparently so similar to Earth evolve in such
L162: a radically different way over the last four
L163: thousand million years?
L164: By the mid-1990s, many ground
L165: observatories and more than twenty
L166: spacecraft had attempted to explore Venus.
L167: A set of orbiters and descent probes - the
L168: Soviet Venera series and the Vega balloons
L169: and landers, the US Mariner, Pioneer Venus
L170: and Magellan missions - tried to penetrate
L171: this hostile world to add pieces to the big
L172: jigsaw that Venus represented for scientists.
L173: Many missions were lost, many landers were
L174: destroyed by the high pressure and
L175: temperature of the Venusian atmosphere
L176: while trying to gather the first information
L177: about the planet. For years, the dense
L178: atmosphere with its thick cloud cover
L179: prevented scientists from seeing what lay
L180: below and from understanding the nature
L181: of the Venusian surface. Only when modern
L182: radar imaging systems became operational
L183: on space probes and at ground
L184: observatories did the first glimpses of the
L185: real face of Venus start to emerge.

L239: (1983-1984), and NASA’s Magellan radarmapping mission (1990-1994) together
L240: provided a comprehensive picture of an
L241: arid world, with landscapes shaped by
L242: intense volcanic and geological activity.
L243: There were vast plains marked by lava
L244: flows, bordered by highlands and
L245: mountains. The later discovery of the nightside thermal emissions from deep inside
L246: the atmosphere of Venus provided an
L247: effective tool with which to peek through
L248: the dense clouds and study the lower
L249: atmospheric layers. The Galileo and Cassini
L250: spacecraft were the first to use this
L251: approach during their short fly-bys en route
L252: to Jupiter and Saturn.
L253: Despite this past intensive exploration of
L254: the planet, our knowledge of Venus is still
L255: very limited. Almost all of the planet’s
L256: peculiar features remain unexplained, and
L257: so a new phase of exploration is long
L258: overdue. This important scientific call has
L259: been picked up by Europe and, after being
L260: forsaken for a decade, the ‘Morning Star’ will
L261: receive a new visitor in the form of Venus
L262: Express, an orbiter mission developed by
L263: the ESA and due for launch in October
L264: 2005.
L265: Thanks to a set of state-of-the-art
L266: instruments for planetary investigations,
L267: Venus Express will delve into the secrets of
L268: the Venusian atmosphere. It will study its
L269: complex dynamics and chemistry, and the
L270: interactions between the atmosphere and
L271: the surface, which will provide clues about
L272: the surface’s characteristics. It will also study
L273: the interactions between the atmosphere
L274: and the interplanetary environment (solar
L275: wind) to improve our understanding of the
L276: planet’s evolution.
L277: In the most comprehensive study ever of
L278: the Venusian atmosphere, Venus Express
L279: will address many unanswered questions:
L280: • How do the complex global dynamics
L281: of the planet work?
L282: What causes the super-fast
L283: atmospheric rotation and the
L284: hurricane-force winds?
L285: What maintains the double
L286: atmospheric vortex at the poles?
L287: • How does the cloud system work?
L288: How do clouds and haze form and
L289: evolve at different altitudes?
L290: What is at the origin of mysterious
L291: ultraviolet markers at the cloud tops?
L292: • What processes govern the chemical
L293: state of the atmosphere?
L294: • What role does the ‘greenhouse effect’
L295: play in the global evolution of the
L296: Venusian climate?
L297: • What governs the escape processes of
L298: the atmosphere?
L299: • Are there water, carbon-dioxide or
L300: sulphuric-acid cycles on Venus?
L301: • What caused the global volcanic
L302: resurfacing of Venus 500 thousand
L303: million years ago?
L304: • Why are some areas on the surface so
L305: reflective to radar?
L306: • Is there currently volcanic or seismic
L307: activity on the planet?

L317: In the sidereal dance of the planets, Venus
L318: reaches its closest point to Earth every
L319: nineteen months. At the next approach, ESA
L320: will be ready to launch Venus Express to the
L321: star-bright planet. The launch window will
L322: open on 26 October 2005, and close one
L323: month later on 24 November. Everything
L324: has been planned to exploit the planet’s
L325: proximity to make the journey as short as
L326: possible.
L327: A Russian Soyuz-Fregat launcher will boost
L328: Venus Express into space from the Baikonur
L329: Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. The Soyuz
L330: rocket will lift the autonomous upper stage
L331: ‘Fregat’ , with Venus Express mounted on
L332: top, into a sub-orbital trajectory. Then, with
L333: two consecutive burns, Fregat will inject the
L334: spacecraft onto an interplanetary or ‘escape’
L335: trajectory that, with few corrections, will
L336: take it directly to Venus.
L337: For about five months (162 days), Venus
L338: Express will cruise in the peace of space.
L339: Once at Venus, in April 2006, it will fire its
L340: main engine to slow down and counteract
L341: the predominant pull of the Sun and of
L342: Venus, to be captured into orbit around the
L343: planet. A large velocity change is required
L344: for the initial capture manoeuvre, which will
L345: require the engine to burn for 53 minutes.
L346: Starting about five days later, a two-weeklong series of manoeuvres will put the
L347: spacecraft into its final operating orbit,
L348: circling the poles of the planet once every
L349: 24 hours. At its closest, the spacecraft’s orbit
L350: will drop to 250 kilometres altitude over
L351: northern latitudes, and at its furthest it will
L352: be 66 000 kilometres from the planet’s
L353: surface.
L354: To Venus in record timeTo Venus in record time

L357: The orbit of Venus Express has
L358: been specifically chosen to learn as
L359: much as possible about the planet
L360: and to maximise the scientific return
L361: from the mission. It prescribes an
L362: ellipse which is ‘locked’ in space with
L363: respect to fixed stars, while the planet
L364: slowly rotates below it. During the
L365: course of the first full Venusian day
L366: (243 Earth days), the spacecraft will
L367: make a global observation from orbit of
L368: the Venusian atmosphere, of the surface
L369: characteristics and of the interaction with
L370: the solar wind. On the second Venusian day,
L371: Venus Express will have the opportunity to
L372: fill possible observation gaps experienced
L373: in the course of the first day and to study in
L374: more detail items of particular scientific
L375: interest selected during the first day. The
L376: second day also allows observation of how
L377: the phenomena seen on the first day vary
L378: with time.
L379: The spacecraft’s very short distance from
L380: Venus at pericentre (250 kilometres) allows
L381: in particular study of the northern
L382: hemisphere at
L383: very high
L384: resolution. One
L385: specially interesting
L386: feature is ‘Ishtar Terra’ ,
L387: a continent-sized highland
L388: that may provide clues as to whether the
L389: surface of Venus is actually ‘moving’ on
L390: geological time scales. The greater distance
L391: of Venus Express from the planet around
L392: apocentre (66 000 kilometres) will allow
L393: good global coverage of the atmospheric
L394: conditions in the southern hemisphere,
L395: including the tracking of cloud features.

L402: ‘Fast’ is Venus Express’s watchword
L403: Not only will Venus Express reach the planet in a very short time, but the mission has also been developed in an incredibly
L404: short time. Actually, Venus Express is the fastest ESA mission ever developed, taking less than four years from concept to
L405: launch.
L406: In 2001, in consultation with the European scientific community, ESA saw a very favourable and creative opportunity for
L407: planetary research. By reusing the Mars Express spacecraft design and the same industrial team, as well as some of the
L408: scientific instruments developed for Rosetta (mission to study a comet) and Mars Express (the ESA mission to Mars), Europe

L584: Venus rotates in the opposite direction to
L585: Earth, so the Sun appears to rise in the west.
L586: It also rotates very slowly, with one rotation,
L587: or sidereal day, taking 243 Earth days. This is
L588: longer than the Venusian year (orbital
L589: period), which is 225 Earth days long. Its
L590: winds, however, are so fast that they can
L591: circumnavigate the planet in only four Earth
L592: days: it is still not known why this happens.
L593: Venus does not have its own planetary
L594: magnetic field to protect it from the solar
L595: wind. On Earth, the magnetic field is
L596: generated by movements in the metallic
L597: core coupled with the planet’s relatively fast
L598: rotation. On Venus, the core may be solid
L599: and the rotation of the planet is very slow,
L600: which may explain the lack of a magnetic
L601: field, but scientists are still debating the
L602: reasons.
L603: In studying Venus, we are trying to
L604: understand not only how the Solar System
L605: formed and evolved, but also the complex
L606: set of forces and mechanisms that have
L607: caused such dramatic differences between
L608: the internal structures, surfaces and
L609: atmospheres of Venus and Earth. An
L610: understanding of Venus can therefore lead
L611: eventually to a better understanding of our
L612: own planet, and especially the long-term
L613: evolution of Earth’s climate.

L876: Greenhouse effect
L877: On the global scale, Venus’s climate is
L878: strongly driven by the most powerful
L879: greenhouse effect found in the Solar
L880: System. The agents sustaining it are water
L881: vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphuric-acid
L882: aerosols. About 80% of the incoming solar
L883: radiation is reflected back to space by the
L884: cloud layer, and only 10% manages to get
L885: through it and heat the surface. However,
L886: the thermal radiation emitted by the
L887: surface gets trapped by the same
L888: atmosphere. The result is an amazing 500ºC
L889: difference between the surface and cloudtop temperatures. Are there other gases
L890: sustaining such an efficient planetary
L891: greenhouse? How is the heat transported
L892: from the surface to the cloud layer: through
L893: radiation or dynamic mechanisms such as
L894: turbulence? Answering these questions is
L895: one of the primary goals of Venus Express.

L910: possibly to the formation of enormous
L911: cumulus-type clouds. Furthermore, the
L912: upper clouds are marked by areas visible in

L921: Hurricane-force winds and huge
L922: atmospheric vortexes
L923: The lower atmosphere of Venus has a
L924: dramatic and peculiar behaviour pattern. At
L925: the level of the cloud tops, the atmosphere
L926: rotates at a formidable velocity, with wind
L927: speeds of up to 360 kilometres per hour.
L928: The speed of the winds then progressively
L929: decreases to almost zero at the planet’s
L930: surface, where it becomes a gentle breeze,
L931: barely able to kick up dust. What
L932: mechanisms cause this ‘zonal superrotation’? Furthermore, two enormous
L933: vortices, with very complex shapes and
L934: behaviours, rotate vertically over the poles,
L935: recycling the atmosphere downwards. The
L936: vortex at the north pole, the only one
L937: previously observed in some detail, has a
L938: peculiar ‘double-eye’ shape, surrounded by
L939: a collar of cool air. It completes a full
L940: rotation in only three Earth days. How are
L941: the super-rotation and the polar vortices
L942: linked? How does the global atmospheric
L943: circulation on Venus work? No model is so
L944: far able to simulate the dynamics of Venus’s
L945: atmosphere as too few data are available.
L946: Venus Express observations will finally fill
L947: the gaps.

L953: kilometres), above the cloud tops, carbon

L2: Spacecraft bus dimensions

L18: HGA2 = 0.3 m in diameter, 2 low-gain antennas
L19: Structure
L20: The Venus Express spacecraft was a virtual twin of Mars Express. The spacecraft body itself, termed a ‘bus’, was a honeycomb aluminium box about one and a half metres wide. With its solar arrays extended, it measured about eight metres across.
L21: As with Mars Express, the scientific instruments were mounted in the bus. Only minor changes from Mars Express were required to accommodate the revised instruments payload, which was concentrated on three sides of the spacecraft.
L22: However, the environment of Venus is very different from that of Mars. This required some design changes that made Venus Express more suited to operating around Venus.
L23: Thermal control
L24: Flying to an inner Solar System planet like Venus, at half the distance to the Sun as compared to Mars, meant that the effect of solar illumination and ionising radiation on the spacecraft was much higher. In fact, the heating of the spacecraft was four times greater at Venus than at Mars.
L25: To keep Venus Express within temperatures that were safe for the spacecraft, the radiators on the spacecraft surface were increased in area and efficiency. The spacecraft coating, called ‘multi-layer insulation’ or MLI, was composed of 23 layers, packaged differently from Mars Express.
L26: Moreover, for Venus Express, the MLI was gold instead of black, which provided greater capability to reflect radiation away. In general, Mars Express was designed to keep warm while Venus Express was modified to stay cool.
L27: Artist's impression of Venus Express orbiting Venus
L28: Power
L29: At Venus, the Sun appears twice as powerful as on Earth, so solar radiation to power the spacecraft was plentiful. Venus Express’s solar arrays could be made smaller (almost half size) than those of Mars Express.
L30: The two symmetric solar arrays, measuring around six square metres, were based on a ‘triple junction’ gallium arsenide (GaAs) technology, different from the silicon-based technology used for Mars Express.
L31: The solar cells, each composed of four layers of gallium arsenide, were more tolerant to high temperatures (up to around 120 °C), so they were more suitable for hot environments. Moreover, they were able to exploit a wider range of solar radiation. The solar cells were separated by aluminium strips that helped to reject heat. All together, these aluminium strips covered half of the overall solar array surface.
L32: When the spacecraft was in shadow (eclipse) or when its power demand exceeded the capacity of the solar arrays, electrical power was supplied by three lithium-ion batteries that were charged by the solar-generated power.
L33: Propulsion
L34: The gravity of Venus, almost the same as Earth’s, is about eight times higher than that of Mars. This, plus the fact that the gravitational pull of the Sun is stronger at Venus, meant that Venus Express needed more energy to brake and be captured into orbit around Venus.
L35: This energy was provided by part of the 570 kilograms of propellant on board (about 20% more than for Mars Express). The propellant mass was almost half of the overall spacecraft weight!
L36: Major spacecraft manoeuvres, like the injection into orbit around Venus, were performed by firing the main engine located at the bottom floor of the spacecraft, while minor manoeuvres were made using four pairs of thrusters located at the four bottom corners of the spacecraft.
L37: The thrusters were used for small trajectory corrections, spacecraft attitude changes, and to correct the altitude of the Venus Express orbit’s pericentre about every 50 days. In fact, due to the gravitational pull of the Sun while the spacecraft is farther away from the planet, the pericentre naturally drifted upwards at a rate of about 1.5 kilometres per day.
L38: Communications
L39: For a spacecraft in orbit around Venus, it is not always possible to point a single antenna dish at Earth while always keeping the cold face of the spacecraft, hosting delicate instruments, away from the Sun.
L40: To overcome this pointing constraint, Venus Express had two high-gain antennas, mounted on different spacecraft faces. The main high-gain antenna, used for most of the communication with Earth, was a dish measuring 1.3 metres diameter.
L41: The second and smaller high-gain antenna (30 centimetres diameter) was used to communicate with Earth when the spacecraft was in the part of the orbit closest to our planet (less than 0.78 Astronomical Units* away).
L42: Two low-gain antennas were also mounted on board, to communicate with Earth during launch, in the first days of the cruise and, if necessary, during severe ‘safe modes’.
L43: *One Astronomical Unit, defined as the mean distance between the Sun and Earth, is about 150 million kilometres.
L44: Navigation and attitude control
L45: Venus Express was a three-axis stabilised spacecraft. Through three different systems on board, the spacecraft could acquire data about its position in space, attitude (orientation) and change of velocity.
L46: These on-board systems consisted of two star trackers, two Sun sensors and a set composed by three laser gyroscopes and three accelerometers. They provided data to re-orient the spacecraft and the solar arrays when necessary.
L47: The actual spacecraft re-orientation manoeuvre or trajectory correction was performed by means of so-called ‘reaction wheels’ or by firing the thrusters.
L48: Data storage
L49: The Venus Express on-board computer was responsible for supervising and managing the overall spacecraft functioning, for handling all data acquired by instruments and sensors and for sending commands through the whole spacecraft.
L50: Part of the computer was the Solid State Mass Memory, which had a capacity of 12 gigabits. All scientific data collected by the instruments were stored here until they could be downloaded to Earth during the appropriate orbital phase.

L5: Venus Express was ESA's first spacecraft to voyage to our nearest planet; it was built around the design of Mars Express, making it quicker and cheaper to develop. It studied the planet's complex dynamics and chemistry, and the interactions between the atmosphere and the surface, which provided clues about the surface’s characteristics.
L6: It also studied the interactions between the atmosphere and the interplanetary environment (solar wind) to better understand the evolution of the planet. Venus Express also observed the Venusian atmosphere and clouds in unprecedented detail and accuracy.

L8: The Venus Express Mission Operations Centre (MOC) was located at ESOC, Darmstadt, Germany.

L26: The Venus Express Flight Control Team (FCT) consisted of the Spacecraft Operations Manager (SOM) and a team of engineers, analysts and spacecraft controllers, all of whom worked at ESOC.

L29: Mission operations overview
L30: Venus Express was launched on 9 November 2005, at 3:33 UT by a Soyuz-Fregat rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. The three-stage Soyuz launcher lifted the Fregat autonomous fourth stage mated together with Venus Express into a sub-orbital trajectory.
L31: After separation from the Soyuz third stage, a Fregat main engine burn (at an altitude of about 200 kilometres) for around 20 seconds placed the Fregat-Venus Express composite into an almost circular parking orbit. After a coast phase of about 70 minutes in the low Earth orbit, a second Fregat engine burn, lasting 16 minutes, moved the combined craft from the parking orbit onto an escape trajectory, after which the Fregat stage and Venus Express separated.
L32: Cruise orbit
L33: After launch and separation from the last of the four launcher stages, Venus Express spent 153 days in an interplanetary transfer orbit.
L34: After the spacecraft acquired Sun pointing and deployed its solar arrays, some two hours after launch, spacecraft commissioning started, followed by payload health checks. No routine science operations were planned during the cruise phase.
L35: During the cruise to Venus, the spacecraft was contacted daily for health checks and navigation using the High Gain Antenna. The spacecraft was put on an arrival trajectory to Venus with mid-course navigation and a final course adjustment was performed on 29 March 2006 to fine-tune the arrival hyperbola for Venus Orbit Insertion (VOI).
L36: Venus Express orbit insertion
L37: Venus Orbit Insertion
L38: The orbit insertion manoeuvre took place on 11 April 2006. To enable capture of the spacecraft, it was first slewed such that the main engine was aligned in the direction of travel. The main engine burn lasted around 50 minutes and decelerated the spacecraft by approximately 1251 metres/s (~ 4500 km/h).
L39: The spacecraft initially entered a highly elliptical polar orbit with a pericentre of 400 km, an apocentre of 350 000 km and a period of 9 days. To achieve final operational orbit, a series of correction manoeuvres was performed.
L40: Operational orbit
L41: The selected operational orbit is inertially fixed, so that coverage of all longitudes can be accomplished in one Venus sidereal day (243 Earth days). The nominal mission orbital lifetime was two Venus sidereal days (roughly 500 Earth days). Following a series of mission extensions, Venus Express operations continued around the planet, increasing our knowledge about its atmosphere like what happened with the water or the discovery of nitric oxide (see in depth link upright).
L42: The team conducted ESA's first aerobraking operations in 2014.
L43: In late 2014, Venus Express exhausted its fuel supply and was declared complete on 16 December of that year.
L44: Operation phases
L45: There were two different phases for Venus Express in its operational orbit: the Earth Pointing phase and the Observation phase.
L46: Earth Pointing phase
L47: This phase was dedicated to communication with Earth; one of the two High Gain Antennas is oriented toward Earth to allow the uplink of commands and the dump of the stored data during the observation phase. The antenna is selected according to the relative position of the sun, the earth and the spacecraft since so that the spacecraft's cold faces remain always protected from illumination by the Sun.
L48: Further, the main High Gain Antenna, HGA1, is used during three fourths of the mission, when the spacecraft is the most distant from Earth. In the middle of this period, Venus is in superior conjunction. The second High Gain Antenna, HGA2, is used during the remaining one fourth of the mission, when Venus is closer to Earth. In the middle of this period, Venus is in inferior conjunction. The rotation angle around the Earth direction is optimised in order to avoid any having Sunlight fall on the side wall radiators. High-rate communications are performed eight hours per day in X-band in order to transmit to Earth all science data stored in the Solid State Mass Memory.
L49: Observation phase
L50: There were several different modes of observation, depending on the payload configuration and spacecraft orientation. These include:
L51: Nadir pointing - preferably during pericentre pass, but possible on any portion of the orbit; VIRTIS, PFS, SPICAV and VMC may operate in this mode
L52: Limb observation - VIRTIS, PFS, SPICAV and VMC may operate in this mode
L53: Star occultation (SPICAV)
L54: Star occultation (SPICAV/SOIR)
L55: Radio science (VeRa)
L56: Cebreros during commissioning
L57: The ground stations - Cebreros, New Norcia
L58: Immediately after launch, the antenna dishes at Villafranca, Spain (15m), New Norcia, Australia, (35m) and Kourou, French Guiana, (15m) were used for communication and orbit determination.
L59: Communications with Venus Express, once it arrived in orbit around Venus, were provided by the 35m antenna dish located at the ESA ground station at Cebreros near Madrid, Spain. The 35m antenna in New Norcia was used to support the Venus Radio Science Experiment (VeRa).
L60: All data collected during observations were transmitted to Earth for about eight hours a day (one orbit around Venus is one day, or 24 hours, long). Eight hours of transmission corresponded to the downlink of between 100 and 800 megabytes of data, depending on the actual distance between Earth and Venus.
L61: This mission uses SCOS-2000
L62: Ground segment & mission control system
L63: The Venus Express Mission was controlled by the Venus Express Mission Operations Centre (MOC) at ESOC, in conjunction with ESA's DSA-2 deep-space ground station. The baseline operations philosophy was to acquire scientific data primarily during the 95-minute pericentre planetary passes, store the data on-board and downlink it during a single eight-hour pass each day.
L64: Venus Express Mission Operations Centre (MOC)
L65: Throughout all mission phases, the MOC was the primary interface with the spacecraft through the ground stations. It was responsible for monitoring and control of the complete mission. During critical mission phases (which included launch, Venus orbit injection and aerobraking) it also received tracking, telemetry and command support from the ESA ground station located in New Norcia, which is normally used for data takings in support of the Radio Science investigations.
L66: For the complete mission duration (from launch to the end of mission, when ground contact to the spacecraft/payload is terminated), ESOC provided facilities and services to the scientific community for planning and execution of scientific data acquisition. This included generating and providing complete raw-data sets and necessary auxiliary data to the principal investigators.
L67: Venus Express Science Operations Centre (VSOC)
L68: Throughout the mission, the VSOC provided the Venus Express Principal Investigators with the complete sets of raw data acquired from their instruments, and with any other necessary spacecraft data, for further processing and analysis.
L69: The VSOC is located at ESA's ESAC facility in Spain and is responsible for:
L70: Collecting, coordinating and planning all observations requests from the Principal Investigators
L71: Generating and cross checking the instruments command files that are passed to ESOC to be uploaded to the spacecraft
L72: Managing the Planetary Science Archive, where scientific data are made available to the wide scientific community once the 6-month proprietary period by the principal investigators is concluded
L73: Cutaway diagram showing size and location of instruments
L74: The platform and payload
L75: The platform
L76: The Venus Express spacecraft was a virtual twin of Mars Express. The spacecraft body itself, termed a 'bus', is a honeycomb aluminium box about 1.7 m wide, 1.4m height. With its solar arrays extended, it measures about 8 m across. The scientific instruments are mounted in the bus; only minor changes from Mars Express were required to accommodate the revised instrument payload, which is concentrated on three sides of the spacecraft. However, the environment of Venus is very different from that of Mars, notably, it is much hotter. This required some design changes to make Venus Express more suited to operating around Venus.
L77: The Payload
L78: The Venus Express payload comprised a combination of spectrometers, spectral-imagers and imagers covering a wavelength range from ultraviolet to thermal infrared, a plasma analyser and a magnetometer. This set of instruments is able to study the atmosphere, plasma environment and surface of Venus in great detail. The instruments were provided by collaborative efforts between scientific institutes in ESA member states and Russia. Principal investigators in different European countries lead the nationally funded collaborations.

수성과 금성 탐사에서 강한 열 환경에 대응하는 설계는 어떻게 달랐으며, 그 차이가 관측에 주는 제약은 무엇인가?
## 전체 질문 조사
비교 범위와 열 환경
제공 자료에서 비교할 수 있는 대상은 수성 궤도선 MESSENGER와 금성 궤도선 Venus Express이며, 이를 두 행성의 모든 탐사 방식으로 일반화할 수는 없다. MESSENGER는 태양에서 오는 열과 수성 표면의 재복사열에 대응하기 위해 차양막·방열기·고온 지역 체류를 제한하는 임무 설계를 결합했다. Venus Express는 Mars Express를 바탕으로 더 뜨거운 금성 환경에 맞추어 방열 성능과 단열재, 태양전지 및 통신 장치 배치를 수정했다. 금성에서 우주선이 받는 가열이 화성에서의 4배라는 수치는 금성과 화성의 비교이므로, 수성과 금성 사이의 열 환경 차이를 나타내는 수치로 사용할 수 없다. «수성 | MESSENGER Mercury Orbit Insertion Press Kit (2011)»«금성 | Venus Express ESA Mission Brochure»«금성 | The spacecraft»«금성 | Venus Express operations»

수성: 차양막과 궤도를 결합한 열 보호
MESSENGER의 차양막은 티타늄 프레임에 고정되며, 앞뒤의 Nextel 세라믹 직물 사이에 여러 겹의 Kapton 단열층을 둔 구조로 설계되었다. 수성이 태양에 가장 가까울 때 차양막 앞면은 370°C에 이를 수 있지만, 차양막 뒤 우주선은 약 20°C에서 작동하도록 설계되었으며 이는 실제 측정 성과를 뜻하지 않는다. 고도 200km에서 수성 표면의 재복사열만으로도 지구에서의 태양 복사 강도의 4배에 이르므로, MESSENGER는 원궤도 대신 타원궤도로 저고도 체류를 줄이도록 했다. 구체적으로 각 12시간 공전 중 뜨거운 표면 위를 저고도로 통과하는 시간을 약 25분으로 제한하는 설계가 제시되었다. «수성 | MESSENGER Mercury Orbit Insertion Press Kit (2011)»

수성: 관측 자세와 거리의 제약
MESSENGER는 관측 중에도 차양막이 항상 태양을 향해야 하므로, 관측 목표에 맞추어 우주선의 자세를 자유롭게 바꿀 수 있는 구조는 아니었다. 장비 역시 수성은 보이면서 태양은 보이지 않는 위치에 장착하고 허용 온도 범위 안에 유지해야 했으므로, 열 보호 조건이 관측 장비의 배치를 제약했다. 타원궤도에서 저고도 체류를 짧게 하는 설계는 가까운 거리에서 관측할 수 있는 구간을 제한하며, MLA의 최대 관측 거리 1,500km라는 장비 한계까지 고려하면 모든 궤도 구간에서 해당 장비로 표면을 관측할 수 있다고 볼 수 없다. 또한 여러 종류의 관측을 서로 다른 궤도 구간에서 수행하면서 수성 태양일 두 번, 즉 지구의 1년에 해당하는 기간 안에 완료해야 한다는 임무 조건도 제시되었다. «수성 | MESSENGER Mercury Orbit Insertion Press Kit (2011)»

금성: 방열·단열·전력계의 고온 대응
Venus Express는 안전한 온도를 유지하도록 우주선 표면 방열기의 면적과 효율을 높이고, Mars Express와 다르게 구성한 23겹의 다층 단열재 MLI를 사용했다. MLI는 Mars Express의 검은색 대신 복사를 더 잘 반사하는 금색을 사용했으며, 자료는 Mars Express가 보온을 지향한 데 비해 Venus Express는 냉각을 유지하도록 수정되었다고 설명한다. 태양전지는 약 120°C까지의 고온에 견디도록 설계되었고, 전지 사이에서 열 방출을 돕는 알루미늄 띠가 전체 태양전지판 표면적의 절반을 차지했는데, 이 온도는 우주선 본체 전체의 작동 온도를 뜻하지 않는다. «금성 | The spacecraft»

금성: 열 보호에 따른 지향과 통신 제약
Venus Express에서는 민감한 관측기기가 있는 저온 면을 태양으로부터 보호하면서 단일 접시형 안테나를 항상 지구로 향하게 하는 것이 불가능한 경우가 있었다. 이에 서로 다른 면에 고이득 안테나 두 개를 배치하고, 지구 지향 단계에서 태양·지구·우주선의 상대 위치에 따라 사용할 안테나를 선택하도록 했다. 통신 중에는 측면 방열기에 태양빛이 닿지 않도록 지구 방향을 축으로 한 회전각도 조정했으므로, 열 보호는 통신 자세와 안테나 선택에 직접적인 조건을 부과했다. 운용은 지구 지향 단계와 관측 단계를 구분하고, 기본 방침상 주로 95분의 근금점 통과 구간에서 과학 자료를 수집해 저장한 뒤 매일 한 차례 8시간 동안 전송하도록 계획했지만, 이 시간들이 열 때문에 정해졌다고 자료가 명시하지는 않는다. «금성 | The spacecraft»«금성 | Venus Express operations»

설계 차이의 의미와 근거의 한계
제공 자료를 종합하면 MESSENGER에서는 차양막의 태양 지향과 표면 재복사열 노출을 줄이는 궤도 설계가 관측 자세·장비 배치·저고도 관측 기회를 제약하는 관계가 구체적으로 드러난다. Venus Express에서는 방열 성능과 반사·단열 구조를 강화하면서 저온 면과 방열기를 보호하는 자세를 유지해야 했고, 이에 따른 제약은 특히 지구 통신 방향과 안테나 선택에서 확인된다. 다만 금성의 열 보호가 개별 관측기기의 시야각, 관측 중단 시간 또는 관측 범위를 얼마나 제한했는지는 제시되지 않아, 두 탐사선의 관측 손실이나 제약의 크기를 정량적으로 비교할 수는 없다. «수성 | MESSENGER Mercury Orbit Insertion Press Kit (2011)»«금성 | The spacecraft»«금성 | Venus Express operations»
